title: Evolving Memory, Learning to Meta-Control:Test-Time Adaptation for Experience-augmented LLM Agents

paper.title: Evolving Memory, Learning to Meta-Control: Test-Time Adaptation for Experience-augmented LLM Agents
paper.abstract:
Abstract Self-evolving agents accumulate experience from task streams, but existing frameworks typically rely on fixed pipelines to retrieve and utilize this experience, neglecting when and how to deploy it. We introduce Online Meta-Control of Experience ( OMCE ), a framework that updates experience memory and learns a meta-control policy from task feedback during test-time adaptation. OMCE employs a lightweight contextual-bandit meta-controller that uses compact retrieval signals to select among four cognitive actions—DIRECT, EPISODE, GUIDE, and DISTILL. This routing mechanism operationalizes three coupled decisions: whether to invoke experience, which memory format to utilize, and when to consolidate new guidance. OMCE evolves online, leveraging task feedback to update the memory bank and refine the routing policy via contextual bandit updates.
Experiments on four online adaptation benchmarks across four backbones show that OMCE improves first-attempt success by up to 20.5 percentage points over the strongest compared baseline, while reducing per-task token use by a factor of 5.7–62.5 relative to ACE with GPT-5.2.
Controlled ablations further support the benefits of learned routing and continued routing policy adaptation.

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: Experience-oriented self-evolving LLM agents turn interaction feedback into reusable experience for later tasks Gao et al. (2025) ; Fang et al. (2025a) ; Chen et al. (2026) . This experience can preserve concrete task cases or take more abstract forms, including reasoning guidance, reusable skills, and context playbooks Fang et al. (2025b) ; Ouyang et al. (2025) ; Wang et al. (2023) ; Zhang et al. (2025a) . Its availability, however, does not guarantee its utility for the current task: semantic similarity alone may retrieve unhelpful experience Zhang et al. (2026b) . Even when experience is useful, concrete cases retain execution details but may not transfer readily to different tasks, while distilled guidance captures reusable principles but can omit details needed for execution Fang et al. (2025b) ; Ouyang et al. (2025) . Extending this memory also poses a further choice: distilling guidance from accumulated episodes may help future tasks, but also incurs additional computational cost and can lead to excessive memory growth Zhang et al. (2025a) . These trade-offs leave open how experience should be used and expanded as tasks arrive. Figure 1: From Fixed Pipelines to Learned Meta-Control. Up: Existing methods typically follow a fixed routine for using and consolidating experience, even when the retrieved experience does not help the current task. Down: OMCE learns from task feedback when to use experience, whether to draw on past cases or general guidance, and when to distill new guidance. We argue that scheduling accumulated experience is a learnable dimension of self-evolution, and make it precise through three requirements. (1) Adaptive invocation : whether experience is needed at all Fang et al. (2025b) ; Ouyang et al. (2025) . (2) Selective form : which of its forms to use Fang et al. (2025b) ; Zhang et al. (2025a) . (3) Learnable consolidation : when to distill transferable guidance from episodic evidence Zhang et al. (2025a) ; Shinn et al. (2023) . Meta-control research on adaptive tool use Li et al. (2025) and cognitive-demand monitoring Scoville et al. (2026) suggests that adapting reasoning effort to task demands can be more effective than uniformly allocating computation De Sabbata et al. (2024) .These frameworks, however, control external, fixed resources such as a tool set or a reasoning budget. Accumulated experience differs: the agent produces it itself, in heterogeneous forms, in a store that grows and shifts, so scheduling it requires a decision over use and consolidation, not a single invocation flag. To this end, we propose Online Meta-Control of Experience ( OMCE ), an agent framework that learns to control experience use and consolidation through a lightweight meta-controller over episodic and guidance memory. Implemented as a contextual bandit, the controller regulates whether to invoke experience, which form to use, and when to distill new guidance (Fig. 1 ). At inference, it summarizes retrieval profiles in a nine-dimensional meta-state vector and uses linear reward models to select among DIRECT, EPISODE, GUIDE, and DISTILL, without an additional LLM call for action selection. After execution, memory evolution records outcomes, generates case-specific insights, and refines injected guidance using task feedback, while meta-evolution adapts the routing policy through online bandit updates. Experiments on four online adaptation benchmarks show that OMCE achieves the highest first-attempt success in most evaluated settings, with competitive cumulative success under the same retry budget. Ablations show that no fixed experience strategy is consistently the best, while controlled comparisons with shared memory demonstrate the value of learning when and how to use experience. Freezing the controller reduces first-attempt success, supporting continued policy adaptation as memory evolves. Finally, efficiency analysis shows that OMCE achieves a favorable performance–token trade-off, using substantially fewer tokens than ACE’s full-playbook prompting.

sections.heading: Experience Memory and Self-Evolving Agents.
sections.text: Experience-augmented reasoning has advanced LLM-agent memory systems from case-level trajectory retrieval Fang et al. (2025b) ; Shinn et al. (2023) to structured agentic knowledge bases Tang et al. (2025) ; Xu et al. (2025) . Other work stores reusable plans, skills, or heuristics for cross-task transfer Wang et al. (2023) ; Wu et al. (2024) ; Chen et al. (2025) ; Allard et al. (2026) , or distills experience into general principles, evolving playbooks, and reusable reasoning memories through generation, reflection, and refinement Zhao et al. (2024) ; Zhang et al. (2025a) ; Ouyang et al. (2025) . MemRL Zhang et al. (2026b) improves retrieval by scoring memory candidates with a non-parametric Q-value function, and Evo-Memory Wei et al. (2025) benchmarks retrieval, integration, and update in continuous task streams. Overall, these efforts show that experience can be accumulated, abstracted, and maintained in multiple forms. However, most frameworks still use a fixed retrieve-inject-reflect pipeline, with limited control over whether memory is useful for the current task, which type of experience to consult, or whether a new outcome should be consolidated Majumder et al. (2023) ; Yang et al. (2025) .

sections.heading: Meta-Control in LLM Agents.
sections.text: Learned meta-control decides whether to invoke a resource and how much to spend on it: a tool Li et al. (2025) , a deliberation budget De Sabbata et al. (2024) ; Ji-An et al. (2025) , test-time compute Snell et al. (2024) , a learning mode Dupoux et al. (2026) , or a verifier Wan et al. (2026) ; related work also edits the agent’s program directly Zhang et al. (2026a) . Dual-process agents separate fast execution from slower deliberation Evans (2011) ; Evans and Stanovich (2013) ; Liu et al. (2023) ; Zhang et al. (2025b) , and feedback-driven methods improve these meta-level policies with reward signals Wu and Qu (2025) . Closest to our setting are controllers selecting among reasoning strategies at inference time: Meta-Reasoner Sui et al. (2026) learns with a contextual bandit when to backtrack or restart within one problem, and MetaScale Liu et al. (2026) evolves meta-thoughts as the sampling budget grows. Both focus on controlling predefined resources, but OMCE instead learns to manage the experience an agent accumulates over time, jointly deciding when to use existing experience and when to distill new guidance. Figure 2: Architecture of OMCE . The lightweight Meta-Controller selects a cognitive action specifying whether and which experience to inject into the task prompt. The agent solves the task with the augmented context containing the query and any injected experience. Memory evolution records outcomes in episodic memory, distills guidance before execution when DISTILL is selected, and refines injected guidance afterward using task feedback.

sections.heading: 3 Online Meta-Control of Experience
sections.text: Given a sequential stream of queries 𝒬 = { q 1 , … , q N } \mathcal{Q}=\{q_{1},\ldots,q_{N}\} , OMCE equips an LLM agent with Episodic Memory, Guidance Memory, and a Meta-Controller (Fig. 2 ). For each query, the controller uses meta-state to select an action that determines whether and which experience to inject into the task prompt, including whether to distill new guidance before execution. The resulting augmented context is supplied to the agent. Task feedback then updates the stored experience and the controller’s policy, allowing both to adapt across the stream.

sections.heading: 3.1 Memory Representation
sections.text: The Episodic Memory maintains episodic records of past interactions, ℳ epi = { η i } i = 1 N \mathcal{M}_{\mathrm{epi}}=\{\eta_{i}\}_{i=1}^{N} . Each record η i = ( τ i , r i , Ω i ) \eta_{i}=(\tau_{i},r_{i},\Omega_{i}) contains the task trajectory τ i \tau_{i} , the immediate reward r i ∈ [ 0 , 1 ] r_{i}\in[0,1] , and a small set of case-specific insight entries Ω i = { ω i , m } m = 1 M i \Omega_{i}=\{\omega_{i,m}\}_{m=1}^{M_{i}} . These entries capture reusable patterns from successful cases or corrective lessons from failed ones. The Guidance Memory stores guidance entries distilled from related episodic records, ℳ guide = { ψ k } k = 1 K \mathcal{M}_{\mathrm{guide}}=\{\psi_{k}\}_{k=1}^{K} . Compared with ω i , m \omega_{i,m} , each ψ k \psi_{k} is less tied to a single trajectory and instead summarizes a recurring principle that may transfer across similar cases. For retrieval, both case-specific insights and guidance entries use the same two-part format: a compact description of the applicable scenario and a detailed principle. The description serves as the cue for query-to-memory matching, while the principle supplies the content for injection into the task prompt.

sections.heading: 3.2 Adaptive Meta-Control
sections.text: We model the inference-time control process of OMCE as a contextual bandit Chu et al. (2011) ; Abbasi-Yadkori et al. (2011) , in which the Meta-Controller observes the meta-state S t meta S_{t}^{\mathrm{meta}} , selects a cognitive action, and receives feedback only for that action at each step.

sections.heading: Meta-State Representation.
sections.text: To support efficient action selection, the Meta-Controller summarizes the current retrieval results rather than consuming raw memory text. Given the current query q t q_{t} , we retrieve the top- M M candidate entries from each memory source based on cosine similarity between the semantic embeddings of the query and each entry’s applicable scenario Reimers and Gurevych (2019) ; Karpukhin et al. (2020) . We denote the retrieved sets from episodic memory and guidance memory by ℳ epi retr \mathcal{M}^{\mathrm{retr}}_{\mathrm{epi}} and ℳ guide retr \mathcal{M}^{\mathrm{retr}}_{\mathrm{guide}} , respectively. The meta-state is a nine-dimensional feature vector S t meta ≡ x t = ( x t , 1 , … , x t , 8 , 1 ) . S_{t}^{\mathrm{meta}}\equiv x_{t}=(x_{t,1},\ldots,x_{t,8},1). (1) The state captures three properties: Relevance ( x t , 1 , x t , 2 x_{t,1},x_{t,2} ), measured by retrieval scores from the two memory sources; Quality ( x t , 3 , … , x t , 6 x_{t,3},\ldots,x_{t,6} ), measured by memory quality scores and their relevance-weighted counterparts; and Diversity ( x t , 7 , x t , 8 x_{t,7},x_{t,8} ), defined specifically as episodic outcome diversity . Diversity captures the balance between successful and failure-side episodic evidence and the normalized entropy of outcome types, rather than semantic diversity among retrieved entries. The first eight coordinates are normalized online, while the final coordinate is a constant bias; x t , 7 x_{t,7} and x t , 8 x_{t,8} are exposed only to the DISTILL action through an action-specific feature mask. Appendix A gives the full definitions and the quality-score mapping. These three properties inform action selection. High relevance and reliable evidence favor experience reuse, weak or conflicting signals favor DIRECT, and relevant but insufficiently generalized episodes favor DISTILL.

sections.heading: 4 Experiments
sections.text: We evaluate all methods in an online adaptation setting, where tasks arrive and must be solved sequentially. After completing an instance, the agent observes task feedback and may update its memory, controller, or context before processing the next instance.

sections.heading: 4.1 Experimental Design
sections.text: We organize the evaluation around five questions. RQ1 : does learned routing raise first-attempt success across benchmarks and backbones? RQ2 : how should the routing policy be determined, in particular is a fixed form of experience use sufficient, and does a learned controller beat fixed and hand-crafted alternatives? RQ3 : do the gains come from the routing policy, or from the memory content and the update schedule? RQ4 : does the controller keep improving as the stream proceeds? RQ5 : what is the token cost of these gains? Section 4.2 addresses RQ1, Section 4.3 addresses RQ2 to RQ4, and Section 4.4 addresses RQ5. The evaluated methods span four test-time adaptation regimes: no external memory ( Base LLM ), within-instance retry ( Reflexion Shinn et al. (2023) ), cross-task adaptation ( MemP Fang et al. (2025b) ), and cross-task adaptation with multi-attempt inference, including ACE Zhang et al. (2025a) , ReasoningBank Ouyang et al. (2025) and our OMCE , which differs from these baselines in learning when to invoke experience and which form to use rather than following a fixed routine. Against OMCE , we additionally compare policies that always commit to one form of experience and a hand-crafted rule over retrieval scores ( Section 4.3 ). We report two variants of OMCE : OMCE -TS and OMCE -UCB, which implement meta-evolution with two contextual-bandit action-selection algorithms: Thompson Sampling (TS) Agrawal and Goyal (2013) and LinUCB Chu et al. (2011) ; Abbasi-Yadkori et al. (2011) , respectively (detailed in Appendix B ). We evaluate on four complementary benchmarks spanning distinct task domains under this shared setting: BigCodeBench Zhuo et al. (2024) and SWE-bench Verified Jimenez et al. (2023) for code generation and repository-level software engineering, MultiChallenge Deshpande et al. (2025) for realistic multi-turn conversation, and BBEH Kazemi et al. (2025) for advanced general reasoning. Across all benchmarks, we use four LLMs as backbone models: GPT-5.2 OpenAI (2025) , DeepSeek-V3.2 Liu et al. (2025) , DeepSeek-V4-pro DeepSeek-AI (2026) , and Kimi-K2.5 Team et al. (2026) . We use one-shot success rate (OSR) as the primary metric, also called first-attempt success: it measures whether the current policy and accumulated experience solve an instance on the first attempt. For methods with retry mechanisms, we additionally report cumulative success rate (CSR), defined as success within a shared budget of P = 4 P=4 total attempts, including the initial attempt ( Section G.3 ). Reflexion does not transfer experience across instances, so by construction its first attempt matches the Base LLM under this protocol; we therefore report its CSR only, while OMCE ’s CSR combines within-instance retries with cross-instance adaptation. Full details on benchmark construction, trial protocol, baseline implementations, metrics, and controller variants are provided in Appendix G . sections.heading: 4.2 Main Results
sections.text: Table 1 reports the performance across all benchmark-backbone configurations, demonstrating that OMCE systematically improves test-time adaptation: it attains the highest first-attempt success on eleven of the sixteen benchmark–backbone configurations. We highlight two key findings: Learned Routing Leads in First-Attempt Success. OMCE dominates first-attempt success wherever retrieved experience carries reliable signal. On MultiChallenge it leads ReasoningBank, ACE, and MemP on all four backbones, by 13.5 to 20.5 points over the best of the three, and its weakest backbone there, at 67.4%, still exceeds the strongest baseline on any backbone by 10.7 points. It leads the same three baselines on all four backbones of SWE-bench Verified by 1.8 to 10.0 points. On BBEH it matches or leads the strongest baseline on three backbones, reaching 53.3% with GPT-5.2 against 52.4% for ACE and trailing by 0.1 point on Kimi-K2.5. On BigCodeBench, OMCE leads in OSR with GPT-5.2 but trails MemP on the other three backbones. Selective Routing Can Bypass Memory. DIRECT allows the controller to solve a task without injecting retrieved experience. On BigCodeBench, the better-performing OMCE variant matches or exceeds the Base LLM’s OSR on three backbones and trails it by 0.2 point on the fourth. ACE falls 9.9 to 11.1 points below it on three.

sections.heading: 4.3 Ablation Study
sections.text: We examine where the gains of OMCE come from through three questions, answering RQ2 to RQ4 . The first compares routing rules on all four backbones, covering two fixed policies, a hand-crafted one, and the two learned variants: Table 2 reports GPT-5.2 and Appendix D the full grid. The other two examine memory use and controller updates on GPT-5.2, holding the backbone fixed across conditions. Figure 3: Performance–efficiency trade-off on four benchmarks using GPT-5.2. The x-axis represents the one-shot success rate, and the y-axis reports the token cost in log scale (average total prompt and output tokens consumed per task).

sections.heading: How should the routing policy be determined?
sections.text: Fixed- a EPISODE a_{\textsc{EPISODE}} always injects retrieved episodic records into the task prompt, and Fixed- a GUIDE & DISTILL a_{\textsc{GUIDE}\&\textsc{DISTILL}} always reuses or distills guidance. On GPT-5.2, Fixed- a EPISODE a_{\textsc{EPISODE}} exceeds Fixed- a GUIDE & DISTILL a_{\textsc{GUIDE}\&\textsc{DISTILL}} by 7.2 OSR points on BBEH (50.3 vs. 43.1), and the order reverses on MultiChallenge, where Fixed- a GUIDE & DISTILL a_{\textsc{GUIDE}\&\textsc{DISTILL}} leads by 7.7 points (63.7 vs. 56.0). Committing to either form costs accuracy where it fits poorly: Fixed- a EPISODE a_{\textsc{EPISODE}} trails OMCE -TS by 11.4 points on MultiChallenge, and Fixed- a GUIDE & DISTILL a_{\textsc{GUIDE}\&\textsc{DISTILL}} trails it by 10.2 points on BBEH. Which form helps therefore depends on the task; the same reversal appears at the level of individual backbones, where the BBEH ordering of the two fixed policies flips between GPT-5.2 and DeepSeek-V3.2. OMCE -HEU is also adaptive, selecting among the same four actions with fixed thresholds on retrieval scores (Appendix C ). On GPT-5.2 the learned controllers exceed the tuned heuristic by 0.8 to 7.7 points on all four benchmarks, with the widest margin on BBEH (53.3 vs. 45.6). Across the full grid the better learned variant outperforms OMCE -HEU on 14 of the 16 benchmark–backbone pairs. Individually, TS and UCB each outperform OMCE -HEU in OSR on 11 of the 16 configurations.

sections.heading: Do the gains come from routing or from the memory?
sections.text: To separate routing from memory content, we fix the memory that OMCE has built and vary only the routing rule. Always-Both reads both memory types on every task and Random picks a feasible action uniformly, both against that same snapshot. With identical memory content, OMCE exceeds Always-Both by 3.6 to 16.0 OSR points and Random by 4.8 to 11.8, with higher CSR on all four benchmarks, and reaches the best OSR of any policy on the same snapshot. Where the gap is largest, on SWE-bench Verified, Always-Both reaches 48.8 OSR, below the Base LLM without any memory (52.8, Table 1 ), and on BigCodeBench it reaches 47.5 against 48.1. On two of the four benchmarks, then, indiscriminate retrieval is worse than retrieving nothing. The same holds when the memory keeps evolving. Always-Both-and-Update runs the full online loop as OMCE does, but retrieves from both memory types and updates memory after every task, and it trails OMCE on all four benchmarks by 2.2 to 9.8 OSR points, with lower CSR in each case. These comparisons show an OSR advantage for learned routing under both fixed and evolving memory. Figure 4: Self-correction detection in MultiChallenge. The meta-controller routes the query to GUIDE ( a GUIDE a_{\textsc{GUIDE}} ) rather than to episodic cases that enforce the user’s outdated constraint.

sections.heading: Does the controller need to keep learning?
sections.text: We freeze the controller parameters at the midpoint of each stream while memory continues to evolve. The two interventions in this section order the benchmarks identically. Freezing the controller costs first-attempt success on all four, by 5.5 points on MultiChallenge, 3.5 on BBEH, 1.8 on BigCodeBench, and 0.6 on SWE-bench Verified, while OMCE ’s lead over the best fixed policy of Table 2 over the same four benchmarks is 3.7, 3.0, 1.7, and 0.4 points. CSR falls on three benchmarks, by 0.2 to 3.1 points; on BigCodeBench it instead rises, from 59.2 to 65.4. Continued controller updates improve OSR on all four benchmarks, while their effect on CSR varies across benchmarks.

sections.heading: 4.4 Efficiency Analysis: Token–Performance Trade-off
sections.text: We evaluate efficiency using tokens per task , the average total LLM tokens consumed per instance over the full online adaptation pipeline; Section G.3 gives the exact accounting. Figure 3 plots the performance–efficiency frontier with GPT-5.2 as the backbone; Appendix H gives the statistics for all backbones. MemP is the most token-efficient method because it performs no test-time scaling. With GPT-5.2, OMCE reduces per-task token use by a factor of 5.7–62.5 relative to ACE . OMCE sits between the two across all four benchmarks and all four backbone LLMs ( Figure 5 ), at a token cost close to the retrieval baselines.

sections.heading: 4.5 Case Study
sections.text: A case from MultiChallenge illustrates the routing decision ( Figure 4 ): a user planning a conference initially says “in June,” then corrects it to “in July.” A fixed pipeline retrieves insights from the top-matching episodic records, all of which direct the agent to hold earlier statements as hard constraints, and the model accordingly insists on June. The meta-controller reads S t meta S^{\text{meta}}_{t} as weak or conflicting on the episodic side and routes the query to a GUIDE a_{\textsc{GUIDE}} , where the retrieved guidance concerns detecting and reconciling contradictions; the agent then picks up the July date and solves the task.

sections.heading: 5 Conclusion
sections.text: In this work, we presented OMCE , a framework that recasts experience-augmented reasoning from an always-on memory pipeline into a learnable meta-cognitive control problem. Instead of treating retrieval, context injection, reflection, and consolidation as a fixed routine, OMCE employs a lightweight meta-controller based on compact retrieval features and linear reward models to govern the full lifecycle of experience: choosing among DIRECT, EPISODE, GUIDE, and DISTILL. Crucially, this meta-controller evolves online via task feedback, progressively improving the agent’s judgment over its own cognitive processes. Evaluations across four online adaptation benchmarks demonstrate that OMCE establishes state-of-the-art OSR and a favorable performance-token trade-off. Ultimately, our findings suggest that as self-evolving agents mature, the primary bottleneck of online adaptation shifts from merely accumulating richer experience to learning exactly when and how that experience should be deployed and updated.

sections.heading: Limitations
sections.text: OMCE inherently relies on timely feedback. In environments with sparse or delayed rewards, the contextual-bandit updates can become noisy, and abrupt task distribution shifts may render both the accumulated experience and the learned meta-policy stale. Moreover, due to the partial observability of the bandit formulation, the controller lacks counterfactual signals regarding unchosen cognitive routes, potentially slowing its recovery from early suboptimal decisions. Additionally, as the memory banks expand indefinitely, retrieval may suffer from redundancy or semantic collisions. To address these limitations, future work could integrate established memory-maintenance techniques (e.g., explicit aging or eviction of stored memory entries). More fundamentally, future iterations could leverage the LLM’s reflective capabilities to simulate counterfactual rewards for unchosen actions (potentially accelerating bandit convergence), or complement the current meta-control framework with explicit memory auditing and pruning, advancing towards a fully autonomous lifelong-learning agent. Our controlled comparisons of memory use and controller updates focus on GPT-5.2, while the routing comparison spans all four backbones. Testing the same interventions on other backbones would help assess whether the observed effects generalize.

sections.heading: Appendix C Heuristic Baseline Details
sections.text: The heuristic baseline employs a fixed, rule-based policy to select actions based solely on retrieval scores, without any online learning or parameter updates. The decision mechanism evaluates the available signals against predefined thresholds to compute a heuristic score for each possible action, ultimately selecting the action with the maximum score. Let s epi s_{\mathrm{epi}} and s guide s_{\mathrm{guide}} denote the mean retrieval scores for the episodic records and guidance entries, respectively. The heuristic relies on three configurable hyperparameters: the weak threshold τ w \tau_{w} , the use threshold τ u \tau_{u} , and the margin threshold τ m \tau_{m} . To ensure numerical stability, we define a small constant ϵ = 10 − 8 \epsilon=10^{-8} . The heuristic scores for the four actions in the action space 𝒜 \mathcal{A} are computed as follows:

sections.heading: DIRECT ( a DIRECT a_{\textsc{DIRECT}} ).
sections.text: The score for DIRECT is inversely proportional to the maximum available retrieval score, encouraging the agent to skip when all retrieval signals are weak: score DIRECT = max ⁡ ( 0 , 1 − max ⁡ ( s epi , s guide ) max ⁡ ( τ w , ϵ ) ) \text{score}_{\textsc{DIRECT}}=\max\left(0,1-\frac{\max(s_{\mathrm{epi}},s_{\mathrm{guide}})}{\max(\tau_{w},\epsilon)}\right) (17)

sections.heading: G.1 Task Setting.
sections.text: Our experiments follow the online adaptation evaluation setting Zhang et al. (2025a) , where each method processes the test stream in a single sequential pass. For every incoming instance, the agent first produces its prediction using the current policy, memory, or context, observes the task feedback, and then updates the corresponding memory or controller state before moving to the next instance. To make the comparison controlled, all methods use the same task order on each benchmark, the same backbone LLM, and the same evaluation pipeline. Each method is evaluated in a single run over each benchmark–backbone configuration due to the cost of LLM API calls. Reported success rates aggregate outcomes across benchmark instances. For methods supporting retries, each instance allows up to four total attempts, including the initial attempt; these are within-instance retries rather than independent experimental runs. Methods that support multi-attempt inference use a shared budget of P = 4 P=4 total attempts, following Section G.3 , and OMCE may stop early once a task is solved.

sections.heading: G.2 Benchmarks.
sections.text: Under this setting, we consider four complementary benchmarks spanning code generation, repository-level software engineering, realistic multi-turn conversation, and advanced general reasoning. English is the language used for all benchmarks. Code generation and software engineering. BigCodeBench Zhuo et al. (2024) is a function-level code generation benchmark emphasizing complex instructions and diverse function or tool calls, with unit-test-based automatic evaluation to reflect practical programming behavior. SWE-bench Verified Jimenez et al. (2023) is a human-validated subset of SWE-bench designed to assess whether agents can resolve real-world GitHub issues in repository-scale codebases. Multi-turn conversation. MultiChallenge Deshpande et al. (2025) measures whether a model can handle realistic, challenging user interactions over extended dialogue contexts, with particular emphasis on instruction-following, context allocation, and in-context reasoning. We use GPT-4o-mini OpenAI (2024) as the judge model, to judge whether the answer meets the hidden task requirement. Advanced general reasoning. BIG-Bench Extra Hard (BBEH) Kazemi et al. (2025) is a substantially more challenging successor to BIG-Bench Hard (BBH) Srivastava et al. (2023) ; Suzgun et al. (2023) , covering a broad range of general reasoning skills. We use a shuffled 6-task subset comprising 1,200 instances: causal_understanding Nie et al. (2024) ; Kıcıman et al. (2023) , dyck_languages Tyen et al. (2023) , temporal_sequence, web_of_lies White et al. (2024) , word_sorting Tyen et al. (2023) , and zebra_puzzles Shah et al. (2024) . These instances are mixed and randomly shuffled to construct the evaluation stream.

sections.heading: G.3 Evaluation Metrics.
sections.text: We adopt one-shot success rate ( OSR ) as the primary evaluation metric, defined as the fraction of test instances solved correctly on the first attempt during online adaptation. This metric directly measures the agent’s immediate response quality under its current policy and accumulated experience. When multiple attempts are allowed, we additionally report cumulative success rate ( CSR ), defined as the fraction of instances solved within a maximum budget of P = 4 P=4 total attempts, including the initial attempt. This corresponds to at most three retries after the initial attempt. For methods without multi-attempt inference, the unavailable metric is marked as “-” in the result tables. Since Reflexion Shinn et al. (2023) improves later attempts through within-instance self-reflection rather than cross-task experience transfer, we report it under CSR in the main comparison. To measure inference efficiency, we report tokens per task , the average total LLM tokens consumed per instance. This count includes all LLM calls made throughout the full online adaptation pipeline for a task, rather than only the final task-solving call; in particular, it includes token usage from auxiliary stages such as memory update and other adaptation-related inference, as well as additional token consumption introduced by test-time scaling in baselines that use it. The average is computed by dividing the total token consumption by the total number of tasks. Token accounting includes the cost of solving tasks and the cost of extracting and refining experiences, but excludes evaluator or judge-model calls.

sections.heading: G.4 Baselines and Methods.
sections.text: For baselines and compared methods, we include a Base LLM and four representative test-time improvement approaches that enhance performance without parameter updates. These baselines separate test-time scaling alone, cross-task experience transfer alone, and methods that combine cross-task adaptation with multi-attempt inference. Base LLM. Base LLM is evaluated on each benchmark without any external memory, i.e., the model is queried with the benchmark’s default prompt template (as provided by the dataset authors) and produces an answer directly. Reflexion Shinn et al. (2023) . Reflexion instantiates test-time scaling through within-instance self-reflection over repeated attempts. After an attempt, the agent converts task feedback into a natural-language self-reflection and conditions subsequent attempts on these reflections. In our comparison, Reflexion does not transfer experience across different test instances. MemP Fang et al. (2025b) . MemP transfers experience across tasks but makes only a single attempt per instance. It therefore represents cross-task experience transfer without multi-attempt inference. ACE Zhang et al. (2025a) . ACE treats prompts/contexts as evolving playbooks and improves them through a modular generate-reflect-curate loop with structured, incremental updates designed to prevent context degradation across iterations; ACE supports both offline prompt optimization and online adaptation via memory/context updates driven by execution feedback. ReasoningBank Ouyang et al. (2025) . We evaluate ReasoningBank in its sequential MaTTS setting, where the method combines cross-task adaptation with multi-attempt inference. OMCE (ours). OMCE combines memory evolution with online meta-evolution. OMCE -TS uses Thompson Sampling Agrawal and Goyal (2013) , while OMCE -UCB uses an optimistic LinUCB-style rule Chu et al. (2011) ; Abbasi-Yadkori et al. (2011) . Appendix B gives the formal specifications, and Appendix E analyzes the optimistic variant.

sections.heading: Appendix H Detailed Efficiency Results
sections.text: Figure 5 reports tokens per task , as defined in Section G.3 , across four backbone LLMs (GPT-5.2, Deepseek-V3.2, Deepseek-V4-pro, and Kimi-K2.5) on four benchmarks. Lower values indicate better inference efficiency. (a) GPT-5.2 (b) Deepseek-V3.2 (c) Deepseek-V4-pro (d) Kimi-K2.5 Figure 5: Performance–efficiency trade-off on four benchmarks using GPT-5.2, Deepseek-V3.2, Deepseek-V4-pro, and Kimi-K2.5 as backbone LLMs. The x-axis shows one-shot success rate, and the y-axis shows token cost (log scale), defined as the average total number of prompt and output tokens consumed per task. The figure reveals a clear and consistent pattern across all four backbone models. Base LLM and MemP are the most token-efficient methods because they eschew test-time scaling, and therefore add limited overhead beyond direct inference. ReasoningBank and OMCE incur a moderate additional token budget due to retrieval, reflection, and structured online adaptation, but remain far more efficient than large-context prompting. By contrast, ACE is dramatically less efficient: relative to OMCE , it requires about 62.5 × \times more tokens per task on BigCodeBench, 32.5 × \times more on SWE-bench Verified, 5.7 × \times more on MultiChallenge, and 21.8 × \times more on BBEH. This inefficiency is consistent with ACE’s strategy of unconditionally injecting the entire playbook into the prompt, which substantially inflates the context length as adaptation proceeds. Taken together with Figure 3 , these results place OMCE between the two extremes on every benchmark and backbone: more accurate than the token-cheap baselines, and far cheaper than ACE.

sections.heading: Avoiding Harmful Experience ( django-16560 ).
sections.text: In this task, the objective is to add a violation_error_code parameter to Django’s BaseConstraint . When forced to use guidance entries, the model is misled by irrelevant rules (e.g., "Wrong-Layer Patch Trap") and applies patches to the wrong abstraction layer, resulting in failure. However, the Meta-Controller accurately calculates low retrieval scores for both episodic records and guidance entries, confidently selecting DIRECT ( a DIRECT a_{\textsc{DIRECT}} ) (confidence 1.0). By proceeding without hallucinated guidance, OMCE successfully solves the task, demonstrating its ability to protect the model from harmful or irrelevant memory.

sections.heading: Selecting the Right Experience Type ( django-13401 ).
sections.text: This task requires modifying the equality semantics of abstract model fields so they do not compare as equal across different models. This is a highly sensitive task where EPISODE fails because specific past cases do not generalize well to core equality logic. Conversely, GUIDE succeeds. The Meta-Controller successfully identifies this distinction, routing the task to a GUIDE a_{\textsc{GUIDE}} . This highlights the critical importance of selecting the appropriate experience type for tasks that require architectural guidance rather than specific implementation details.

sections.heading: DISTILL ( django-13809 ).
sections.text: The goal of this task is to add a --skip-checks option to the runserver command. The baseline model without experience fails to correctly wire the option through the execution flow. The Meta-Controller observes that while there are highly similar episodic records available, there are no directly applicable guidance entries. Consequently, it selects DISTILL ( a DISTILL a_{\textsc{DISTILL}} ) to create a new guidance entry from the retrieved episodic records. The newly distilled guidance entry correctly instructs the model on the appropriate modification layer, leading to a successful resolution. This showcases OMCE ’s capability to dynamically generate new guidance entries when existing experience is insufficient.

sections.heading: Appendix J Broader Impact
sections.text: This work introduces Online Meta-Control of Experience ( OMCE ), a framework designed to improve the efficiency and reliability of self-evolving LLM agents. The ability to selectively ignore misleading or redundant past experiences helps mitigate the propagation of errors in memory-enhanced agent systems. This contributes to the development of more robust AI assistants. However, like all frameworks that enhance the autonomy and efficiency of AI agents, OMCE could potentially be repurposed for malicious activities. While OMCE offers a pathway toward more intelligent and resource-efficient agents, its deployment should be accompanied by continuous monitoring and safety protocols to ensure that its evolutionary capabilities remain aligned with ethical standards and human values.

We introduce Online Meta-Control of Experience ( OMCE ), a framework that updates experience memory and learns a meta-control policy from task feedback during test-time adaptation. OMCE employs a lightweight contextual-bandit meta-controller that uses compact retrieval signals to select among four cognitive actions—DIRECT, EPISODE, GUIDE, and DISTILL. This routing mechanism operationalizes three coupled decisions: whether to invoke experience, which memory format to utilize, and when to consolidate new guidance. OMCE evolves online, leveraging task feedback to update the memory bank and refine the routing policy via contextual bandit updates. Experiments on four online adaptation benchmarks across four backbones show that OMCE improves first-attempt success by up to 20.5 percentage points over the strongest compared baseline, while reducing per-task token use by a factor of 5.7–62.5 relative to ACE with GPT-5.2. Controlled ablations further support the benefits of learned routing and continued routing policy adaptation. † † footnotetext: * Equal contribution. † \dagger Corresponding authors. 1 Introduction Experience-oriented self-evolving LLM agents turn interaction feedback into reusable experience for later tasks Gao et al. (2025) ; Fang et al. (2025a) ; Chen et al. (2026) . This experience can preserve concrete task cases or take more abstract forms, including reasoning guidance, reusable skills, and context playbooks Fang et al. (2025b) ; Ouyang et al. (2025) ; Wang et al. (2023) ; Zhang et al. (2025a) . Its availability, however, does not guarantee its utility for the current task: semantic similarity alone may retrieve unhelpful experience Zhang et al. (2026b) . Even when experience is useful, concrete cases retain execution details but may not transfer readily to different tasks, while distilled guidance captures reusable principles but can omit details needed for execution Fang et al. (2025b) ; Ouyang et al. (2025) . Extending this memory also poses a further choice: distilling guidance from accumulated episodes may help future tasks, but also incurs additional computational cost and can lead to excessive memory growth Zhang et al. (2025a) . These trade-offs leave open how experience should be used and expanded as tasks arrive. Figure 1: From Fixed Pipelines to Learned Meta-Control. Up: Existing methods typically follow a fixed routine for using and consolidating experience, even when the retrieved experience does not help the current task. Down: OMCE learns from task feedback when to use experience, whether to draw on past cases or general guidance, and when to distill new guidance. We argue that scheduling accumulated experience is a learnable dimension of self-evolution, and make it precise through three requirements. (1) Adaptive invocation : whether experience is needed at all Fang et al. (2025b) ; Ouyang et al. (2025) . (2) Selective form : which of its forms to use Fang et al. (2025b) ; Zhang et al. (2025a) . (3) Learnable consolidation : when to distill transferable guidance from episodic evidence Zhang et al. (2025a) ; Shinn et al. (2023) . Meta-control research on adaptive tool use Li et al. (2025) and cognitive-demand monitoring Scoville et al. (2026) suggests that adapting reasoning effort to task demands can be more effective than uniformly allocating computation De Sabbata et al. (2024) .These frameworks, however, control external, fixed resources such as a tool set or a reasoning budget. Accumulated experience differs: the agent produces it itself, in heterogeneous forms, in a store that grows and shifts, so scheduling it requires a decision over use and consolidation, not a single invocation flag. To this end, we propose Online Meta-Control of Experience ( OMCE ), an agent framework that learns to control experience use and consolidation through a lightweight meta-controller over episodic and guidance memory. Implemented as a contextual bandit, the controller regulates whether to invoke experience, which form to use, and when to distill new guidance (Fig. 1 ). At inference, it summarizes retrieval profiles in a nine-dimensional meta-state vector and uses linear reward models to select among DIRECT, EPISODE, GUIDE, and DISTILL, without an additional LLM call for action selection. After execution, memory evolution records outcomes, generates case-specific insights, and refines injected guidance using task feedback, while meta-evolution adapts the routing policy through online bandit updates. Experiments on four online adaptation benchmarks show that OMCE achieves the highest first-attempt success in most evaluated settings, with competitive cumulative success under the same retry budget. Ablations show that no fixed experience strategy is consistently the best, while controlled comparisons with shared memory demonstrate the value of learning when and how to use experience. Freezing the controller reduces first-attempt success, supporting continued policy adaptation as memory evolves. Finally, efficiency analysis shows that OMCE achieves a favorable performance–token trade-off, using substantially fewer tokens than ACE’s full-playbook prompting. 2 Related Work Experience Memory and Self-Evolving Agents. Experience-augmented reasoning has advanced LLM-agent memory systems from case-level trajectory retrieval Fang et al. (2025b) ; Shinn et al. (2023) to structured agentic knowledge bases Tang et al. (2026) , or distills experience into general principles, evolving playbooks, and reusable reasoning memories through generation, reflection, and refinement Zhao et al. (2024) ; Zhang et al. (2025) benchmarks retrieval, integration, and update in continuous task streams. Overall, these efforts show that experience can be accumulated, abstracted, and maintained in multiple forms. However, most frameworks still use a fixed retrieve-inject-reflect pipeline, with limited control over whether memory is useful for the current task, which type of experience to consult, or whether a new outcome should be consolidated Majumder et al. (2023) ; Yang et al. (2025) . Meta-Control in LLM Agents. Learned meta-control decides whether to invoke a resource and how much to spend on it: a tool Li et al. After completing an instance, the agent observes task feedback and may update its memory, controller, or context before processing the next instance. 4.1 Experimental Design We organize the evaluation around five questions. RQ1 : does learned routing raise first-attempt success across benchmarks and backbones? RQ2 : how should the routing policy be determined, in particular is a fixed form of experience use sufficient, and does a learned controller beat fixed and hand-crafted alternatives? RQ3 : do the gains come from the routing policy, or from the memory content and the update schedule? RQ4 : does the controller keep improving as the stream proceeds? RQ5 : what is the token cost of these gains? Section 4.2 addresses RQ1, Section 4.3 addresses RQ2 to RQ4, and Section 4.4 addresses RQ5. The evaluated methods span four test-time adaptation regimes: no external memory ( Base LLM ), within-instance retry ( Reflexion Shinn et al. (2023) ), cross-task adaptation ( MemP Fang et al. (2025b) ), and cross-task adaptation with multi-attempt inference, including ACE Zhang et al. (2025a) , ReasoningBank Ouyang et al. Instead of treating retrieval, context injection, reflection, and consolidation as a fixed routine, OMCE employs a lightweight meta-controller based on compact retrieval features and linear reward models to govern the full lifecycle of experience: choosing among DIRECT, EPISODE, GUIDE, and DISTILL. Crucially, this meta-controller evolves online via task feedback, progressively improving the agent’s judgment over its own cognitive processes. Evaluations across four online adaptation benchmarks demonstrate that OMCE establishes state-of-the-art OSR and a favorable performance-token trade-off. Ultimately, our findings suggest that as self-evolving agents mature, the primary bottleneck of online adaptation shifts from merely accumulating richer experience to learning exactly when and how that experience should be deployed and updated. Limitations OMCE inherently relies on timely feedback. In environments with sparse or delayed rewards, the contextual-bandit updates can become noisy, and abrupt task distribution shifts may render both the accumulated experience and the learned meta-policy stale. Moreover, due to the partial observability of the bandit formulation, the controller lacks counterfactual signals regarding unchosen cognitive routes, potentially slowing its recovery from early suboptimal decisions. Additionally, as the memory banks expand indefinitely, retrieval may suffer from redundancy or semantic collisions. To address these limitations, future work could integrate established memory-maintenance techniques (e.g., explicit aging or eviction of stored memory entries). More fundamentally, future iterations could leverage the LLM’s reflective capabilities to simulate counterfactual rewards for unchosen actions (potentially accelerating bandit convergence), or complement the current meta-control framework with explicit memory auditing and pruning, advancing towards a fully autonomous lifelong-learning agent. Our controlled comparisons of memory use and controller updates focus on GPT-5.2, while the routing comparison spans all four backbones. Testing the same interventions on other backbones would help assess whether the observed effects generalize.
